questions.content: Describe two actions taken by the United States between 1947 and 1949 to stop the spread of communism in Europe. Give a detail to support each action. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] First action identified, e.g. the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan or the creation of NATO.
[1] Accurate supporting detail, e.g. the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 promised support for countries resisting communism and gave about 400 million dollars of aid to Greece and Turkey; the Marshall Plan (announced June 1947) offered economic aid to rebuild Western Europe, around 13 billion dollars from 1948 to 1952.
[1] A second, different action identified.
[1] Accurate supporting detail, e.g. NATO was formed in April 1949 as a military alliance of the United States, Canada and Western European states, in which an attack on one member was an attack on all; the Western powers airlifted supplies to West Berlin in 1948-49.
Accept other valid actions and accurate detail.

questions.content: Explain how the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 increased tension between the Soviet Union and the Western powers. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Germany and Berlin were divided into four occupation zones after 1945, with Berlin lying deep inside the Soviet zone.
[1] In 1948 Britain, France and the United States combined their zones and introduced a new currency, the Deutschmark, which the Soviet Union saw as a threat to its position.
[1] In June 1948 Stalin cut road, rail and canal links to West Berlin, hoping to force the Western powers out of the city.
[1] The Western powers organised the Berlin Airlift, flying in food and fuel for almost a year, which showed their determination and made the Soviet Union appear aggressive.
[1] The blockade ended in May 1949 without the Soviet Union achieving its aim, and the crisis hardened the division of Germany into West Germany (the Federal Republic, 1949) and East Germany (the German Democratic Republic, 1949).
[1] The blockade pushed the Western states towards military alliance, leading to NATO in April 1949, and increased mutual fear and mistrust.
Accept other accurate, relevant points.

questions.content:
Source A: a diary entry (an imagined diary written for this paper by a schoolteacher living in West Berlin; treat it as a genuine diary for the questions)

Saturday 18 September 1948. Another night of the aircraft. They pass over the roof every few minutes, and we have stopped noticing them, as one stops noticing a clock. Today we received our ration of dried potato and powdered milk, and the neighbours shared what coal they had. The children at school were given a small piece of chocolate that fell from a plane, and you would think it was gold. People say the Russians will give up before the winter. I am not so sure. Some in the street say we should have accepted their terms and had food from the east, but most say they would rather be cold and free. I am tired, but I find I am proud of us.

Assess the value and limitations of Source A for a historian studying how people in West Berlin experienced the blockade. Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Origin: a private diary entry by a schoolteacher in West Berlin written in September 1948, during the blockade, so it is a first-hand account.
[1] Purpose: a personal record not intended for publication, so the writer is likely to be honest rather than writing propaganda.
[1] Value: the content gives detail of daily life, e.g. rationing of dried potato and powdered milk, shared coal, and aircraft overhead, which matches what is known about the airlift.
[1] Value: it shows a range of opinion (some wanted to accept Soviet terms; most preferred to be 'cold and free') and the mood of the people.
[1] Limitation: it is the view of one person, in one part of the city, on one day, so it may not represent everyone, e.g. workers, families in other districts or people who favoured the Soviet side.
[1] Limitation: it covers only the first months and cannot show how the blockade ended or how people felt later; the writer's pride may reflect her own opinion.
Accept other valid points about origin, purpose, value and limitation.

questions.content:
Source B: a table of statistics (constructed for this paper; all figures are approximate and rounded)

Approximate number of people leaving East Germany for the West each year

1950: about 200,000
1953: about 330,000
1956: about 280,000
1960: about 200,000
January to August 1961: about 155,000

Note: many of those leaving were young and skilled workers, such as doctors, engineers and teachers.

Source C: part of an imagined official statement issued by the East German government on 13 August 1961 (written for this paper)

The working people of our republic have long suffered from the activities of enemy agents and those who lure our citizens away with promises of easy riches. To defend peace and protect our state, the borders of the capital will from today be closed and guarded. These measures are directed against no honest citizen, only against those who seek to damage our country.

Compare what Source B and Source C suggest about why the Berlin Wall was built in 1961. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Source B shows that very large numbers of people, many of them skilled, were leaving East Germany, which suggests the government faced an economic and political problem.
[1] Source C claims the borders were closed to protect the state from enemy agents and from people luring citizens away, so both sources suggest the government wanted to stop people leaving.
[1] Difference: Source B gives neutral figures that point to dissatisfaction with life in East Germany, whereas Source C is an official justification that blames outside enemies and does not mention the refugees.
[1] A supported judgement, e.g. Source B is more reliable about the real cause, the loss of workers, while Source C shows the reason the government wished to give the public; neither explains the Soviet Union's role or the Western reaction.
Accept other valid comparisons.

questions.content:
Source D: a letter (an imagined letter written for this paper by an American teenager in Florida to her cousin, 25 October 1962)

We have practised hiding under our desks twice this week. Dad listened to the president on the radio on Monday night and Mum has been buying tins of food. At school everyone is pretending it is a joke, but nobody is laughing very much. They say Russian missiles are on Cuba and that our navy is stopping ships. We can almost see Cuba on a clear day, or it feels that way. I do not think they will really use them. Please write back soon.

What can a historian learn from Source D about the impact of the Cuban Missile Crisis on ordinary Americans? Mention one limitation of the source. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] A valid inference about fear or anxiety, e.g. families were frightened and prepared for the possibility of war.
[1] Supported by evidence from the source, e.g. 'hiding under our desks', Mum buying tins of food.
[1] A valid inference about how the news reached the public, e.g. through the president's radio address on Monday 22 October, and the public knew about the naval blockade or quarantine.
[1] A limitation, e.g. it is the view of one teenager in one place near Cuba, so it may not represent all Americans; or it was written before the crisis ended on 28 October.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content: Explain why the Cuban Missile Crisis ended without war in October 1962, and one way it changed relations between the superpowers afterwards. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Background: in October 1962 American spy planes found Soviet nuclear missile sites being built in Cuba, after the Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961 and the Cuban Revolution of 1959.
[1] President Kennedy chose a naval blockade, which he called a quarantine, of Cuba (announced on 22 October and in force from 24 October) rather than an immediate air strike or invasion, which allowed time for talks.
[1] Both leaders, Kennedy and Khrushchev, were aware of the danger of nuclear war and exchanged messages.
[1] On 28 October Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles from Cuba; in return the United States promised not to invade Cuba.
[1] The United States also secretly agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey, which allowed Khrushchev to claim a compromise.
[1] Consequence: a direct telephone hotline between Washington and Moscow was set up in 1963, and the Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed in 1963, showing both sides wanted to reduce the risk of nuclear war.
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Do not credit more than the marks available.

questions.content:
'The main reason the Cold War developed between 1945 and 1949 was the clash between American and Soviet ideas and aims in Europe.'

To what extent do you agree with this statement? Use your own knowledge and refer to other causes in your answer. (10 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Explains the ideological clash, e.g. American capitalism and democracy against Soviet communism, and the mutual mistrust it caused.
[1] Considers Soviet control of Eastern Europe, e.g. communist governments installed in Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia (1948) and others, and Churchill's 'iron curtain' idea.
[1] Considers disagreements at the wartime conferences, e.g. Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July to August 1945) over Germany and Poland.
[1] Considers American actions such as the Truman Doctrine (March 1947), the Marshall Plan and the Soviet reaction to them, e.g. the Cominform.
[1] Considers the effect of the atomic bomb and American possession of it, and the Soviet test in 1949.
[1] Considers the division of Germany and the Berlin Blockade (1948 to 1949) as evidence of growing hostility.
[1] Considers the role of leaders and their fears, e.g. Stalin's desire for a buffer zone after huge Soviet losses in the Second World War.
[1] Weighs the clash of aims against at least one other cause, giving reasons.
[1] Shows links between causes, e.g. fear after Eastern Europe's takeover led to American aid, which increased Soviet suspicion.
[1] Reaches a clear, supported judgement about the extent of agreement, using accurate dates, names and terms in a logical structure.
Accept other valid arguments, provided they are supported by accurate evidence.
